facts.value: Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 to Cabinet, 24 June 2026. Report of the Finance and Resources Portfolio Holder (Councillor Flood). 4-page report (doc 40677) plus 2-page Prudential Indicators Annex (doc 40676). Treasury advisors: MUFG Corporate Markets. Read in full from local PDFs on 2026-08-16. The annex carries the numbers; the report body sets the narrative.
facts.note: Officer block on page 4 names only 'L Swanborough Ext: 8527' — no email address, no explicit S151 title. Portfolio holder Cllr Flood. No named S151 in the paper; recipient line for the email is the blocker. Companion annex (doc 40676) held and read alongside the report.

facts.value: TIES TO THE POUND. Our file (price_book.py --find 'Test Valley' → TEST VALLEY BOROUGH COUNCIL) holds 2 PWLB annuity loans totalling £5,789,685 outstanding principal at 2026-03-31, weighted 2.2385%. The annex prints (page 1) 'Gross debt 5,790' in £'000 — £5,790,000. £5,789,685 rounds to £5,790k at £'000 resolution. Match at the paper's rounding. The two loans: PW508571 ANNUITY matures 2044-02-14 at 2.23% (£4,459,036 live balance at 2026-08-14); PW509175 ANNUITY matures 2044-04-24 at 2.27% (£1,200,081 live balance at 2026-08-14).

source.title: Annex page 1 (Gross debt line, £5,790k) against price_book.py --as-at 2026-03-31

facts.note: Both loans are 20-year annuity PWLB maturing early 2044 — a well-below-market pair (weighted 2.24% vs today's 20y certainty rate 6.38% per notice 314/26 PM, 2026-08-14). One of the cleanest reconciliations in our library. Safe to open the email with this line.

facts.value: CHECKED AND CLOSES. At 31/03/26 the annex prints CFR c/f £5,854k and Gross debt £5,790k. The report and annex disclose no PFI or finance-lease long-term liability, and the annex's 'External Debt in year' has been 0 in every year shown, consistent with a single stock of long-dated PWLB and no OLTL. On that basis: £5,854k CFR - £5,790k external borrowing - £0 OLTL = £64k internal borrowing (residual). The CFR is essentially fully externally funded — internal borrowing is immaterial.

source.title: Prudential Indicators Annex page 1 (CFR c/f, Gross debt)

facts.note: Unusual shape. Most councils use their cash pile to fund a substantial share of the CFR internally, keeping external borrowing low. Test Valley has chosen the opposite: keep the PWLB in place (borrowed at 2.24%) AND hold £108.7M of investments earning 4.62%. Positive carry of ~2.38% on the £5.79M spread is worth ~£138k/yr, and sits inside the £918k positive variance on the interest-income side. Deliberate, sensible while the below-market PWLB stands.

facts.value: £108.7M principal invested at 31/03/26, up from £90.3M at 31/03/25 (+£18.4M, +20.4%). Rate of return 4.62% for the year, benchmark 3.86%, variance +0.76%. Monthly benchmark exceeded in every month of 2025/26 (report para 4.2). All investments managed in-house (para 4.1). Attributed to 'long term investments taken out at higher rates before the rates declined through the year'.
facts.note: Achieved +87bp above Bank Rate (Bank Rate finished 2025/26 at 3.75% per report para 5.2). Book is fixed-heavy: only ~£11.2M of the £108.7M is in call/notice, the rest is term. Long-dated locks were the driver of the outperformance.

facts.value: £97.5M of the £108.7M investment book (89.7%) sits in fixed-rate, fixed-term deposits with other local authorities for periods up to five years (report para 4.4, page 2). The remaining £11.2M is in call and notice accounts with access ranging from immediate to 32 days' notice. Test Valley is a large lender into the inter-authority market — on the OTHER side of the market that many of the councils we have read are borrowing from.
facts.note: Cross-sector context: many of our reads this batch (Wiltshire £100m from eleven councils in four months; Liverpool £118m of term money from 17 councils; Bradford £161m from other councils; Gloucestershire 4.15% cheapest LA-to-LA borrowing we've seen; Blackburn with Darwen paid 8.50% for four days to Cornwall) are on the borrower side of this same market. Test Valley is a rare read from the lending side — Wandsworth, Wolverhampton and Enfield have similar shape. Implied yield on the LA portion is ~4.7% (backing out call/notice at ~3.75%: (4.62%×108.7 - 3.75%×11.2) / 97.5 ≈ 4.71%). Rough, but consistent with 1-5y LA rates we see quoted.

facts.value: -37.8% for 2025/26 actual (annex page 1), deeper negative than the -37.2% forecast for the same year. Prior year (2024/25 actual) was -24.9%. Forward estimates: -38.0% (2026/27), -26.2% (2027/28), -21.1% (2028/29) — the ratio moderates as the forecast CFR unwind normalises. Negative ratio means investment income exceeds borrowing costs — Test Valley is a net earner from treasury.
facts.note: Report para 6.2 explains the convention: 'A negative figure shows that investment income is greater than borrowing costs.' -37.8% is one of the most negative financing-cost ratios in our library. Peer context (of the councils we've read this year): Westmorland and Furness ('Not borrowing paid you twice this year'), Enfield ('Your whole investment outperformance is one loan'), and Wandsworth ('the lender on the other side of a market nobody publishes') have similar directional shape but differ in scale.

facts.value: 2025/26 capital expenditure £12.491M actual against £18.023M forecast (annex page 1) — a £5.5M undershoot; every pound financed in year, no unfinanced capex. CFR c/f: £5,885k (31/03/25) → £5,854k (31/03/26 actual) → £11,453k (31/03/27 estimate) → £5,230k (31/03/28 estimate) → £5,002k (31/03/29 estimate). Driver of the 2026/27 spike: Internal Debt in year +£5,817k, reversed the following year with -£6,000k. External Debt in year stays 0 across the whole horizon. Capital programme steps up to £34.808M in 2026/27 then back to £18.681M in 2027/28.

source.title: Prudential Indicators Annex page 1 (Capital Expenditure and CFR waterfall)

facts.note: The 2026/27 CFR bulge is entirely internal — no external borrowing planned. Presumably a receipt or grant lands in 2027/28 (-£6,000k Internal Debt in year) that unwinds the interim funding-from-reserves against the £34.8M capex year. Treasury outturn paper does not name the driver; the capital programme paper for the same meeting cycle (doc 40673/40687) would be where it sits. Not raised as a concern — it is entirely internal and reverses.

facts.value: All prudential indicators complied with. Authorised Limit £20,000k and Operational Boundary £20,000k throughout 2025/26 and the three-year horizon; actual gross debt £5,790k — significant headroom (£14.2M unused against a £20M limit). Fixed rate exposure limit 100% and variable 50% not tested. Investments >364 days limit £35,000k (excluding LAs, and capped at 50% of portfolio at time of placement) — not tested externally. Gross debt (£5,790k) < CFR + 3 years movement (£5,885k) by £95k. Report para 3.2 confirms compliance.

source.title: Prudential Indicators Annex pages 1-2; report para 3.2

facts.note: No indicator breach. No indicator relaxation. The limits are set to numbers well above actual — the £20M authorised limit sits ~£14M above actual gross debt. Comfortable position.

facts.value: Bank Rate cuts of 0.25% in May, August and December 2025/26 took the headline rate from 4.50% to 3.75% by year end (report para 5.2). Two of the three cuts occurred in the same month as the Bank of England published its Quarterly Monetary Policy Report. Bank Rate today (2026-08-16) is still 3.75% — no further Bank Rate cut in the four-and-a-half months since Test Valley's year end. The paper does not quote a forward Bank Rate view.
facts.note: The paper is unusually restrained on forecasts — no rate view expressed, no expected Bank Rate path published. Report para 9.3: 'It does not propose any changes in respect of Treasury Management in the future.' A quiet, healthy report.

facts.value: Interest on investments actual 2025/26 £5,318k against original budget £4,400k (+£918k / +20.9%) and revised February 2026 forecast £5,226k (+£92k / +1.8%). Report para 4.6 attributes to 'long term investments taken out at higher rates before rates declined, and higher than budgeted cash balances available for investment'. Summary bullet on page 1 leads with the £92k above-forecast figure.

source.title: Report para 4.5-4.6 and summary bullet (pages 1 and 3)

facts.note: The £918k against original budget is the more striking figure but the report leads with £92k against the more recent revised forecast — a candid choice. Long-dated LA deposits locked at higher rates before Bank Rate came down are the driver.

summary.text:
A 4-page treasury outturn report to Cabinet on 24 June 2026, with a 2-page prudential-indicators annex. Report of the Finance and Resources Portfolio Holder (Cllr Flood); officer L Swanborough named without email. Treasury advisors MUFG Corporate Markets. Read in full from local PDFs (report doc 40677, annex doc 40676).

The loan-book file ties to the pound. Our price_book.py holds 2 PWLB annuity loans for Test Valley totalling £5,789,685 outstanding at 31/03/26, weighted 2.2385% — PW508571 at 2.23% maturing 2044-02-14 and PW509175 at 2.27% maturing 2044-04-24. The annex prints 'Gross debt 5,790' in £'000. £5,789,685 rounds to £5,790k. One of the cleanest reconciliations in the library, with the whole external-debt story sitting in those two below-market loans.

Balance-sheet identity closes with essentially no internal borrowing. CFR c/f at 31/03/26 £5,854k, external £5,790k, no OLTL disclosed (and the 'External Debt in year: 0' line across every year of the annex is consistent with a single long-dated PWLB stock and no PFI/leases). Residual internal borrowing £64k — the CFR is fully externally funded. Unusual: most councils fund a large share of the CFR internally from the cash pile. Test Valley has chosen to keep the PWLB (borrowed at 2.24%) AND hold £108.7M of investments earning 4.62% — positive carry of ~2.38% on the £5.79M spread is worth ~£138k/yr, and sits inside the £918k positive variance on the interest-income side.

The interesting side of the story is the investment side. £108.7M principal invested at year end, up from £90.3M — a £18.4M increase in the year. Rate of return 4.62%, benchmark 3.86%, variance +0.76%; monthly benchmark exceeded in every month of the year. Of the £108.7M, £97.5M (89.7%) sits in fixed-rate, fixed-term deposits with OTHER LOCAL AUTHORITIES for periods up to five years — Test Valley is on the LENDER side of the inter-authority market that many of our other reads this batch (Wiltshire, Liverpool, Bradford, Gloucestershire, Blackburn with Darwen) are on the borrower side of. Implied yield on the LA portion is roughly 4.71% backing out ~£11.2M in call/notice at ~3.75%.

Financing cost ratio -37.8% actual for 2025/26, deeper negative than the -37.2% forecast for the same year. Investment income exceeds borrowing costs; Test Valley is a net earner from treasury. One of the most negative ratios in our library. Series: -24.9% (24/25 act) → -37.8% (25/26 act) → -38.0% (26/27 est) → -26.2% (27/28 est) → -21.1% (28/29 est). The moderation forward reflects the forecast CFR bulge in 2026/27 (£5,854k → £11,453k, driven by £5,817k of internal debt for a £34.8M capital year, unwound by -£6,000k in 2027/28) — entirely internal, no external borrowing planned across the four-year horizon.

Prudential indicators all complied with. No breach, no relaxation. Authorised limit £20M against actual gross debt £5.79M — £14.2M unused. Bank Rate ended 2025/26 at 3.75% (cuts in May, August, December from 4.50%); still 3.75% today (2026-08-16), no further cut in ~4.5 months since year end. Report para 9.3 explicitly proposes no changes to treasury management going forward — a quiet, healthy outturn.

Signal: none (verified quiet). Nothing in the paper flags a distress or watch item. The interesting cross-sector angle is that Test Valley is one of very few councils we've read whose story is on the LENDING side of the inter-authority market rather than the borrowing side. The lead for the email is the tie-to-the-pound reconciliation combined with the shape observation: two PWLB annuities at 2.24% plus £97.5M lent out at ~4.7% is a rare shape.

Recipient line is the blocker — no officer email published in the paper. Drafted, waiting on an address.

officer.body:
Dear [ADDRESSEE],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Outturn you took to Cabinet on 24 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your outturn is quiet and clean and the annex prints enough for the balance-sheet identity to close in a way most papers don't allow, so this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The first thing worth saying is that our PWLB file for Test Valley ties to your annex to the pound. We hold two annuity loans totalling £5,789,685 at a weighted 2.24% — PW508571 at 2.23% maturing February 2044 and PW509175 at 2.27% maturing April 2044. Your annex prints gross debt of £5,790k. Same number at your £'000 rounding, and the whole external-borrowing story in two loans.

What that leaves is a more interesting observation than most outturns give. Your CFR closes at £5,854k against gross debt of £5,790k, with no PFI or lease liability disclosed and no external-debt movement in any year of the annex. Residual internal borrowing is about £64k — essentially none. Your CFR is fully externally funded. Most councils use their cash pile to internally borrow against the CFR; you've done the opposite, keeping the below-market PWLB in place AND holding £108.7m of investments. The carry is about 2.4 points on the £5.79m spread, worth roughly £138,000 a year that sits inside your £918k above-budget on interest income. On today's twenty-year certainty rate of 6.38% (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August), those two 2044 annuities are 4.14 points below where you'd refinance them.

The more striking figure is on the other side. Of your £108.7m at year end, £97.5m sits in fixed-term deposits with other local authorities up to five years, and only £11.2m in call or notice. That puts Test Valley on the LENDING side of a market we've been watching mostly from the other direction. Of the councils we've read this batch, Wiltshire has taken £100m from eleven councils in four months, Liverpool £118m of term money from seventeen, and Gloucestershire is paying 4.15%, the cheapest LA-to-LA rate we've seen this year. Backing your call/notice out at Bank Rate suggests your LA portion is earning around 4.7% — which reads as being on the more lucrative end of that same market. That's a shape we've read from only a handful of councils, and where pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity gets most useful is showing where that curve has moved month-to-month against the councils actually drawing.

The financing-cost ratio underlines it: -37.8% for 2025/26 on your annex, against a -37.2% forecast. Investment income exceeds borrowing cost by a wide margin, and of the councils we've read this year it's one of the most negative — a way of saying you're one of the few whose treasury function is a net contributor rather than a net cost.

One caveat we owe you on our loan-analysis page. It prices a council's PWLB book against the DMO's premature-repayment curve every day, and yours today shows a net indicative discount of about £1.08m on the £5.66m still running. That's roughly 19% and it looks headline-grabbing, but for a book at 2.24% against a 6.38% market it isn't a windfall — it's the DMO's mark-to-market loss on unwinding your cheap position. Only the DMO can quote for real, and we don't model MRP or accounting treatment. The page is pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis if you want to look.

Standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark work is becoming central to how the whole strategy is framed. Your CFR steps to £11,453k in 2026/27 and back to £5,230k the year after, entirely on internal debt movement — precisely the shape an interactive liability benchmark is best at making visible, and a version tied to our live rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four look most relevant. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is the one — it speaks directly to your £97.5m of term deposits with other councils. PWLB strategy in a rising-rate window covers the below-market loans you hold. Reading the quarterly & outturn reports (for members) is written for the Cabinet members this report goes to. Liability benchmark modelling for treasury covers the 2026/27 CFR bulge. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
